Responding to complexity

Mr H's month is broken. What would a genuinely person-led response look like, and how much can it actually fix?

Three ideas today: support has to start from what matters · “person-led” draws on six distinct concepts, not one word · ask of every response what changes, for whom, with what support, and towards what matters to him.

Contemporary Issues | Week 4Assessment 1
Open · 5 minutes · Assessment 1

Route A is this week

Component 1 · 30%

An individual, narrated PowerPoint, maximum ten slides, due 6 November 2026. It needs critical engagement with evidence, at least two recommendations, and a reference slide with at least five good academic sources. Exact wording and the marking grid are on Brightspace.

Route A, in the handbook's words

“Shared decision making in people of all ages with a long-term condition is key to promoting self-management. How can this process be put into place for a specific group of people to maintain their wellbeing?”

Routes B and C

B: one contagious disease in a high-income and a low-income country (Unit 6). C: frailty in older adults, globally and locally (Unit 5). Today still shows you how a route is argued.

Hands: which route are you drawn to right now, A, B, C, or not yet?
Route A needs a specific group. Mr H helps us think about people with similar needs; he is not the assessment. Whichever route you choose, today models how to support and qualify an argument. For Route A, the chain to show is: a shared decision → an agreed, workable way of managing → the life the person is trying to keep.
Contemporary Issues | Week 4Mr H returns
Mr H returns · 8 minutes

Mr H's month is broken

Fictional case for teaching

What you found

Journeys that did not need to be separate. Advice from one pathway cutting across another. Work nobody had counted.

Three kinds of burden

What his conditions do. What managing them costs. What the organisation of care adds on top.

What you could not do

Fix any of it. That was deliberate. Today you can.

One word or phrase: what matters most to Mr H?
Lecturer: take five or six from the room and write them on the board. Do not correct any of them. You will get “better breathing”, “diabetes control”, “staying out of hospital”.
Contemporary Issues | Week 4His own words
Now ask him · teaching vignette, imagined voice

What matters to you?

Compare that with the board. Several of the things that matter to him sit outside any one clinical pathway. And his breathing matters to him for something.
Contemporary Issues | Week 4Outside the clinic
Idea 1 · why the first question matters · 3 minutes

Most of living with it happens outside the clinic

After the appointment

Mr H leaves the diabetes review at 11:40 with a changed dose, a leaflet and a date. Then: two buses home, the old box still on the shelf, the pharmacy a bus away, a rehab class on Thursday, a benefits letter unopened. The appointment was twenty minutes. The condition is the other 10,060 minutes of the week.

The current version

Care should respect “a person's most precious resource, their time, energy and attention”, and be minimally disruptive. Chief Medical Officer for Scotland, 2024–25. And Scotland's polypharmacy review opens: what matters to the individual?

The appointment is twenty minutes. The condition is the rest of the week. Asking what matters is where every response starts, and it is not the response.
Lecturer: take three. You want the two separate journeys to the same building; and somebody saying “the COPD would still be there”.
Contemporary Issues | Week 4Your board
Idea 2 · before the vocabulary

What would you do for him?

Route one · everyone

One thing you would change in Mr H's month, starting from what he said matters. Not a diagnosis this time; a response. One line.

Route two · optional

Something you have seen a service do for someone like him that helped. Or that did not. No names.

Every question today has two routes. The first is from Mr H, open to everyone. The second is from work or placement, and nobody has to take it.
Keep the board. First we test what you suggested. Then we name the approaches most of it draws on. Some of it will need other services entirely, and one idea can do several things at once.
Contemporary Issues | Week 4The test
Idea 3 · the test, before the vocabulary · 10 minutes

Sort your board: what changes, and for whom?

A change can do more than one thing: reduce his work, move some of it, help him manage it, give him more say. Often two at once. For each thing on your board: what changes, and for whom?

Reduces his work: possible readings

One review instead of three. Someone who takes on the coordination. Help with the damp or the benefits claim. The work still exists; less of it is his.

Moves work: ask whose, and whether it is manageable

To a professional, with time and support: his load drops. To his sister, without asking: hers rises. An app or a diary can be useful support or another demand; it depends how it is used.

Changes who decides, or builds his capacity

He chooses which appointments. He agrees the target with the nurse. A session that takes an hour now and makes the medicines manageable later.
The question to keep all day: whose work has changed, and whether the new arrangement is manageable and worthwhile. Last week's scale still applies, and most changes depend on something: a video call removes two bus journeys if he has a device and data, and adds work if he does not.
Lecturer: go down the board item by item. Take hands for each effect; allow more than one. Open the three reveals only after the sort, as readings, not answers. Push on "what does it depend on" every time.
Contemporary Issues | Week 4Six concepts
Idea 2 · the vocabulary, named from your board · 10 minutes

Six approaches we are using. They overlap. They do different jobs.

ConceptIn plain wordsFor Mr HWhat it changes
Shared decision-makingThe person and the professional decide together, about one decision.Agreeing how tight his sugar target should be, given his life.Who decides
Care and support planningOne plan for the whole person, that they helped write and that gets reviewed.His three conditions, the damp and the money on one page.What happens
Self-management supportHelp with the work the person is already doing every day.A nurse who teaches him the rescue pack and rings a week later.His capacity
Self-directed supportIf assessed as needing social care, a say in how the money is used. Scottish law.Choosing how any support is arranged, and what each option asks of him.Choice and control over how support is arranged
Co-productionPeople who use a service help design it, not just comment on it.Men like him deciding where and when the rehab class runs.Who designs
Integrated careServices organised to work as one around the person.For example: someone who can see his whole month; one record; one contact.How services work together
Match each thing on your board to one of the six. Some will match two. Some will need other services entirely.
Six different jobs. Name the approach, and explain what changes for the person.
Contemporary Issues | Week 4Not synonyms
The guardrail, said once · 5 minutes

They overlap. They are not synonyms.

Which two are easiest to confuse?

Shared decision-making with care planning; self-management support with self-directed support. The difference each time is what it changes for the person, not what it is called.

Care and support planning

In practice: a written set of agreed actions, who will do each one, and when it will be reviewed. Several of the other approaches can sit inside it.

Each can be done badly

A shared decision that was not shared. Co-production that was consultation with a better name. An integrated structure nobody in his flat can feel.

Put the same test to every one of them: what it changes, and for whom.

Contemporary Issues | Week 4Self-management
Block 2 · self-management, properly · 5 minutes

More than behaviour change: three kinds of work, for life

Van de Velde et al. (2019), building on Corbin and Strauss. If self-management is reduced to behaviour change, support can easily become advice about what the person should do rather than support for the work they are already carrying.
Last week's three burdens asked where the demands come from. These three kinds of work describe what living with the conditions involves. Information helps with the first. The other two need support.
Contemporary Issues | Week 4Same plan two people
The hinge · the same plan, two people · 3 minutes, then the plan itself

The same plan, two people

Mr H

Two buses. No car. Redundant, waiting on a decision. Some weeks short of food. Damp flat. Sister across town, working full time. Depression.

Someone else, same three conditions

A car. A partner at home. Savings. A job with flexible hours. A dry house.

Hand both of them the same plan, the same app, the same goal sheet. What would make it easier or harder for each of them?
Lecturer: take two on the first question, then put the second one to the room. That second question is Hardman, and it is why equity is not a footnote this week.
Contemporary Issues | Week 4The plan
The hinge · the plan itself · 9 minutes

The same plan, line by line: support, demand, or depends?

In pairs, three minutes. Mark each line for Mr H, then for the other man: support (gives back more than it costs him), demand (costs him more than it gives back), or depends (say on what). Then we reveal, line by line.
03:00
Fictional teaching artefact — not a real plan · Respiratory Service · COPD self-management plan · Mr HOur answer, and why · yours can differ if your reason is good
1.Take your preventer inhalers twice a day, every day. Rinse your mouth after.
Mr H: Support A small daily job that keeps his breathing settled.Other man: Support The same: small cost, big return.
2.Keep your rescue pack at home. Start it if you are more breathless for two days, or your sputum changes colour. Tell the practice within 48 hours.
Mr H: Depends On his own, it turns on being taught when to start it and on his call being answered.Other man: Support A partner who notices a bad spell, and a phone that works.

Mr H: Demand Breathless and done by Wednesday: one more job, for now.Other man: Support Energy, time and a dry house: it builds strength.

Mr H: Demand Worth a lot for breathing, but twelve trips across town by bus, breathless.Other man: Support Still twelve sessions, but he drives and can move his hours.
5.Contact the stop-smoking service.
Mr H: Depends “Contact” gives him the job. It tips to support if the service contacts him.Other man: Support It matters for his breathing, and the call is easy for him.

Mr H: Demand Another daily task, in a low week.Other man: Depends He has the evenings for it, but it only helps if someone reads it.

+Then adapt it. Cross out one line. Change one. Add one line of support that would make the rest possible for him.
Cross out the diary: a weekly call can ask the same questions. Change rehab to a class nearer home, or a home programme with phone check-ins. Add a named nurse who rings him in week one, with a direct number.
Lecturer: model line 1 and reveal it. Three minutes in pairs. Then lines 2 to 7, one at a time: hands for Mr H, one reason, the other man, then reveal. Every line is work; the label is which way the balance tips. Activity and rehab go from demand to support; the rescue pack and stop smoking from depends to support; the diary from demand to depends; lines 1 and 7 do not change. Last: what would they add? Nearly always a person. Then reveal the adaptation. Say: support is still work; the other man can carry it.
Contemporary Issues | Week 4Who can take it up
The hinge, continued · can support help, and who can reach it?

It can help. And who takes it up?

It can help

Structured, tailored support does more than information alone: working through problems together, following up, agreeing goals, monitoring symptoms. Dineen-Griffin et al. (2019), 58 studies, mostly single-condition primary care.

But who takes it up?

People in lower socioeconomic groups were consistently less likely to take part. Where outcomes were measured, findings were mixed: some narrowed the gap, some made no difference, one widened it. Without tailoring and attention to barriers, it may reinforce the gradient. Hardman et al. (2020).

Support helps when it is structured and followed up. It reaches the people who need it most least often. Both findings go into any design for Mr H.
Lecturer: take three. You want near him, no separate journey, someone who knows his circumstances, not at nine in the morning.
Contemporary Issues | Week 4The worked example
In depth 1 · a real decision, from real guidance · 10 minutes for this and the next two

Agreeing Mr H's HbA1c target

The words first

HbA1c is a blood test that shows average blood sugar over the last two to three months. A target is the level the team and the person aim for. Tighter can mean fewer complications over years; it can also mean more medicines, more checks, and more risk of sugar dropping too low. We are not choosing his number. We are examining how a target should be discussed and agreed.

What the guidance says

NICE's diabetes guideline (NG28; England's guidance, used here as the example) says: agree an individual HbA1c target with the person, and consider using NICE's decision aid for that conversation. The aid lays out, for each target level, what it may do for long-term risk and what it asks in medicines and side effects. nice.org.uk/guidance/ng28 → tools and resources. BRAN is the general prompt for any decision: benefits, risks, alternatives, and no change for now.

The conversation · fictional, for teaching

Nurse explains the test and shows the aid. Mr H: “What I want is to get out more and see my sister. I'm scared of going low on the bus. I don't want more tablets.” Nurse: explains what each target would ask of him. Agreed: no medicine change for now; a target to revisit in three months; the pharmacy review combined with his prescription trip; a phone call in two weeks.

What in that conversation would you need to see in the record for it to count as a shared decision?
Contemporary Issues | Week 4A real shared decision
In depth 1 · shared decision-making, genuinely

A real shared decision, or a form?

What often gets recorded

“Options discussed. Patient agrees.”

It does not tell us who spoke, what the options were, what mattered to him, or what it cost him to choose. It does not prove a poor conversation. It shows the record cannot tell us.

What NICE describes (NG197)

A collaborative process. People need time. Their preferences may differ from the clinician's. The record shows what mattered to the person and what was agreed, and the decision can be revisited. And the right to be less involved belongs to everyone; never use age as a proxy for not wanting a say.

Rewrite it, from the conversation on the last slide. One or two lines, on paper. Document only what was said and agreed.
02:00

One version, after you have written yours

“Discussed HbA1c options and what each asks, using the NICE aid. Mr H's priority: getting out, seeing his sister. Main concern: going low on the bus; does not want more tablets. Agreed: no medicine change now; revisit target in 3 months; pharmacy review combined with prescription trip; phone call in 2 weeks.”
Lecturer: every element of the model is in the supplied conversation. Praise rewrites that record his priority and concern; challenge any that add a preference he did not state.
Contemporary Issues | Week 4Decision aids
In depth 1 · what the evidence is evidence of · 3 minutes

Strong evidence: about the decision

What decision aids do

A very large Cochrane review, across many different decisions. Better knowledge, more accurate risk perception, feeling informed, clearer values, fewer people left passive, and choices that match what the person values. No increase in regret. Stacey et al. (2024), Cochrane.

And the boundary

Every one of those is about the quality of the decision-making process. That does not by itself establish better health, less inequality, or a less burdensome month, though it can contribute to each. And the review is mostly about adults facing a treatment or screening decision; take care before applying it to other groups. And these are mostly single, discrete decisions: not a month like his.

The Level 9 move: name what the evidence is evidence of.
Contemporary Issues | Week 4Four sentences
In depth 2 · does integration integrate? · the sort · 5 minutes

Four sentences from a partnership report. Which claim is each one making?

Fictional sentences, for teaching. They are the kind of sentence such reports contain.

“The Health and Social Care Partnership was established in April 2016.”

Structure exists. True, and it tells you nothing about what happened next.

“Shared care records now operate across three localities.”

Implementation happens. Something was built. Whether his three clinics use it is a separate claim.

“95% of patients with complex needs have a named contact.”

Experience, maybe. Have a named contact is not use one. A figure counts what it counts. Week 1, back again.

“Emergency admissions fell by 4% over the year.”

Outcomes, possibly. Fell compared with what, and because of what: the partnership, or a mild winter. A change in the count is not evidence of what changed it.
Hands for each sentence: structure, implementation, experience, or outcome?
Four claims that get said as one. Sort them, every time, before you believe a policy document.
Lecturer: sort first, reveal after. Let the room argue about the third sentence; it is the one that catches people.
Contemporary Issues | Week 4Does integration integrate
In depth 2 · does integration integrate? · the evidence · 4 minutes

Four claims, often said as one

Integration in Scotland: since 2016, councils and NHS boards must plan some services together through Health and Social Care Partnerships, which you met in Week 1.
1

Structure exists

There is a partnership, a board, a plan.

2

Implementation happens

Things are actually done differently: shared records, joint teams.

3

People experience coordination

Mr H feels it: one contact, no repeated questions, nothing falling between services.

4

Outcomes improve

Fewer crises, better health, a month he can live.

What the evidence says

A large review of UK and international studies (Baxter et al. 2018): the most consistent evidence is for satisfaction, access and perceived quality; evidence on wider outcomes and cost is inconsistent or limited.

What Scotland can say

Audit Scotland (January 2026): limitations in comprehensive, consistent national performance information make it difficult to assess integration's progress and impact. That is uncertainty, not a verdict of failure.

He may notice coordination, and over time outcomes. A phone call is a sign of coordination, not proof that integration worked.
Lecturer: he may notice coordination (3) and, over time, outcomes (4). A phone call is a sign of coordination, not proof that integration worked.
Contemporary Issues | Week 4Four options
Social care's answers · self-directed support · 5 minutes

Four options, and no default

What self-directed support is. Scottish law since 2014: when a council assesses someone as needing social care, it must offer four ways to receive that support, and explain each. For this example, assume an assessment has found eligible needs. Having long-term conditions does not by itself create an entitlement.
1 Direct payment  ·  2 The person directs the available support  ·  3 The authority arranges the support  ·  4 A mix of the others

1 · Direct payment

The money comes to the person; they arrange the support, manage the money and keep records. The guidance says this can mean more day-to-day responsibility, and the authority must make that clear.

2 · The person directs it

The person chooses what the support is and who provides it; the authority holds and pays the money. Choice without the financial administration of a direct payment.

3 · The authority arranges

The authority arranges the support. Less administration on the person; choice and control should still be supported.

4 · A mix

Different parts of the support under different options, for example a direct payment for one thing and the authority arranging the rest.

The question is not which option he should get. What would each one ask of him?
Contemporary Issues | Week 4Three conversations
Social care's answers · what co-production actually means · 4 minutes

Consultation, shared decision, co-production: the same rehab service, three ways

Consultation

“Here is the new timetable: Tuesdays and Thursdays at the hospital. What do you think?” People comment. The service decides.

Shared decision

“There is a hospital class and a community class. Which fits you?” The person chooses between options that already exist.

Co-production

People who use the service and staff design it together: where it runs, when, how you get there, whether it has to be a class at all. Scotland's SDS guidance describes assessment and planning as a co-produced process ending in a support plan.

Not a ladder from bad to good. Different purposes, different levels of involvement. The failure is calling the first one the third.

Contemporary Issues | Week 4Two frameworks
Apply the test · the policy, on the scale · 2 minutes

Both plans aim to move care closer to home

England · 10 Year Health Plan (2025)

Hospital to community. Analogue to digital. Sickness to prevention.

Scotland · Service Renewal Framework (2025)

Care closer to home. Prevention.

Care closer to home can mean one review at his kitchen table, or “you can manage this at home now” with an app. The policy sentence is the same. What it does to his month depends on what is built underneath it. The same question travels to any setting.
Lecturer: take two. You want transport, someone coordinating, and not simply moving the appointment to a different building.
Contemporary Issues | Week 4Judgement
Judgement · written, then one Evidence Log row · 5 minutes

Which responses would materially change Mr H's month, and which mainly change who does the work, or who decides?

What lets us say so

What you have already met today: NICE and the Cochrane review on decisions; Van de Velde, Dineen-Griffin and Hardman on self-management; Baxter and Audit Scotland on integration. Nothing new arrives now.

What remains uncertain

Whether any of it holds for someone with less capacity than Mr H. Whether the outcomes measured are the ones that matter to him. Further reading on both is in the Sway.

A supported judgement, not a score

Claim, evidence, limit. Your written judgement is also your Evidence Log row for this week.

The required line

One piece of work services stop expecting him to coordinate himself.

Final 2 minutes · carry one question into Unit 5

Mr H is 58. Next week the same complexity meets an 84-year-old living alone.

Before you assume anything

Age increases the likelihood of frailty. Age is not frailty. Do not assume she is frail. What additional questions about function, resilience, independence and risk become important when complexity meets later life?

Before Unit 5

Part C: your judgement, 150 to 200 words, one source, one limitation, one line on capacity. Your named source into the Evidence Log. If you are considering Route A, today's concepts, evidence and activity are directly relevant material to revisit.

Contemporary Issues | Week 4Close
Close · three sentences to remember

What Week 4 leaves you with

1

Start from what matters to the person. Ask; do not assume. Several of the things that mattered to Mr H sat outside any one clinical pathway.

2

Person-led care draws on six distinct concepts. They overlap, they are not synonyms, and each can be done well or badly.

3

Ask of every response what changes, for whom, with what support, towards what matters to the person, and what that depends on.
